newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Investors underestimate risk for OATs.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Investors underestimate risk for OATs.

text.p: Investors may have underestimated the risks involved for French bonds in the upcoming election and the effect this could have on France's entry into European economic and monetary union (EMU), economists said on Tuesday.

Economists said while the latest polls showed the ruling centre-right coalition was likely to win, and there was also confidence in France taking a leading role in EMU, French bonds (OATs) could be taking too much for granted.

"The opinion polls say the centre right is going to be re-elected but with a much reduced majority, which in itself is a warning sign," said Julian Jessop, chief European economist at Nikko Europe in London.
"The Socialists could do better than expected, and the market simply isn't positioned for a Socialist win."

The OAT/Bund ten-year yield spread was likely to remain unchanged if the ruling centre-right coalition were to win, analysts said, although some said it had the potential to widen further into negative territory.

But all indicated the possible dangers of over-confidence in French bonds, saying much good news had already been discounted and the potential risks inherent in EMU and the election were still looming.

"If the centre right manage to consolidate their electoral support then the French markets could do quite well...there would be potential for OATs to outperform Bunds," said Craig Shute, fixed income analyst at Bear Stearns in London.
"But it's too early to be over-confident on the French market at the moment, there's already a lot of good news priced in," he added.
The latest French opinion polls indicate a victory for the ruling centre-right coalition, which would also be positive for French entry into EMU.
The centre-right, under President Jacques Chirac, are generally perceived to be more determined to push through pro-EMU economic policies to make France ready for entry into monetary union on time.
In recent weeks the bond market has relaxed considerably and the French/German ten-year yield gap edged back out to put French bond yields trading 13 basis points below German yields.
"I think the markets have calmed down pretty much and are reflecting a strong perception that the tide has turned in favour of the right," said Steven Englander, economist at Smith Barney in Paris.
"That's key because the left's policy on EMU seems much more fluid."

Most investors said there was not much money to be made out of French bonds at these levels, but if the centre-right were to win the election the long-end of the French market would be the most attractive to investors, they said.
"As the polls approach inevitably it's going to be the short-end that will be hit hardest because the currency will take the strain," Jessop said.
In the longer term some investors and economists said they expected French bonds to gradually close the yield gap as the date for EMU came closer.
"It's hard to see why French bonds would trade at minus 20. The risk would seem to be on the upside and I would imagine as EMU approaches French bonds would converge towards German," Englander said.

If, against the odds, the Socialists, led by Lionel Jospin, snatched a surprise victory, economists said the market would suffer with the yield spread soaring around 30 points into positive territory.
